system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2180-12-23 04:32:00 to 2180-12-25 14:38:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis, hepatitis C, and esophageal varices, was admitted for evaluation of hematemesis and melena. Initial workup revealed a drop in hemoglobin from baseline, leading to concern for upper gastrointestinal bleeding. He was started on octreotide, pantoprazole, and ceftriaxone, and underwent an endoscopy which showed no active bleeding but confirmed grade one esophageal varices. A urinary tract infection due to Enterococcus was identified and treated with a seven-day course of amoxicillin. Due to a history of positive syphilis serology and behavioral concerns, a lumbar puncture was performed; cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed no signs of neurosyphilis, though confirmatory results remained pending at discharge. The patient was monitored for alcohol withdrawal using the CIWA scale but did not require treatment. He was discharged home with instructions to complete antibiotics, undergo a repeat endoscopy in eight weeks, and follow up with his primary care and liver specialists. Medication adjustments included holding lisinopril and furosemide, switching nadolol to bedtime dosing, and adding folic acid.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Other and unspecified alcohol dependence, unspecified
Chronic hepatitis C without mention of hepatic coma
Esophageal varices in diseases classified elsewhere, without mention of bleeding
Internal hemorrhoids without mention of complication
Streptococcus infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site, streptococcus, group D [Enterococcus]

procedures.long_title: Endoscopic control of gastric or duodenal bleeding

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You’re in the hospital because you had some bleeding from your stomach and rectum. Do you remember coming in last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I remember. I was feeling bad—stomach pain and saw blood when I went to the bathroom. I also threw up a little dark stuff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s what we call hematemesis and bloody stools. Your blood pressure was high when you arrived, and your hemoglobin was low, so we gave you a blood transfusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit better now, but my stomach still hurts, especially on the lower right side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked with an ultrasound, and there’s no blockage or clot in your liver’s blood vessels. Your liver does show signs of cirrhosis, which we already knew, and your spleen is a bit enlarged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I’m bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Because of your cirrhosis, you have portal hypertension, which can cause bleeding in the stomach. We’re going to do an endoscopy today to look inside and find the source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you’ll be asleep. It’s very safe. We’ll also check your esophageal varices—we know you have grade I, but we need to make sure they’re not bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. I’ve had that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, the endoscopy is done. Good news—we found a small bleeding spot in your stomach called an AVM, or arteriovenous malformation. We used a special technique called argon plasma coagulation to stop the bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it fixed now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the bleeding has stopped. We also saw some irritation in your stomach from portal hypertension, but no active bleeding there. We took a small biopsy of a nodule, which we’ll check later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more treatment for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ll wait for the biopsy results. For now, we’re keeping you on a stomach acid medication through your IV to help healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on omeprazole before. Can I take that again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once you can eat, we’ll switch you back to oral omeprazole. We also gave you an antibiotic to prevent infection, which is standard with cirrhosis and bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember I had a UTI last time. Is that why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. With cirrhosis, you’re at higher risk for infections, so we’re being cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. Your hemoglobin is stable at 10.2, and your white blood cell count has recovered. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My stomach pain is better too. I only took one tramadol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll keep it available if you need it. Your blood pressure has come down too. We restarted your lisinopril today and will continue your nadolol at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I wasn’t supposed to take blood pressure meds with low blood counts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right, we held them initially. But now that your hemoglobin is stable and you’re not bleeding, it’s safe to restart. Controlling your blood pressure helps your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I ate some toast and didn’t feel sick. No more blood in my stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ll keep monitoring, but you’re healing well. We also checked your alcohol withdrawal score—you scored a 6 last night but now it’s 0, so no medication was needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a drink since that brandy in the morning. I know I need to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important, especially with your cirrhosis and hepatitis C. Drinking makes everything worse. We’ll support you with counseling if you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe later. Right now I just want to get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re preparing for discharge. Your labs are stable, and you’ve had no further bleeding. But we still need one more blood test, which we wanted to check before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can’t I just go home and come back for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ideally, we’d like to see the result first. But if you’re feeling well and understand the risks, you can leave now. Just know the bleeding could come back, and we won’t have that final check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but I really want to go home. I’ll take my meds and avoid alcohol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll discharge you against medical advice. You’ll keep taking omeprazole, nadolol, lisinopril, folic acid, thiamine, and ferrous sulfate. Continue tramadol only if you need it for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the biopsy results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll call you or your sister if there’s anything urgent. Otherwise, your primary doctor will follow up. Please make an appointment with your liver specialist soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember—no alcohol, take your meds, and call us if you see any blood or feel worse. Your sister has your discharge papers and contact info.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your final hemoglobin came back at 10.2, which is stable. I’m glad you’re doing well, even though you left before we could review it together.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for letting me know. I feel strong enough to walk out on my own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re alert, not jaundiced, and your neuro exam is normal—no asterixis. That’s a good sign your liver is coping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up like you said. I don’t want to come back for another bleed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best plan. Take care of yourself, and we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go now. My sister is outside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re discharged. Remember your medications and follow-up. We’ll send the biopsy results to your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doc. I’ll stay in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. Stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis, hepatitis C, and esophageal varices, was admitted after presenting with hematemesis and bloody stools. He was found to have a low hemoglobin and was transfused one unit of packed red blood cells. An endoscopy revealed a bleeding arteriovenous malformation in the antrum, which was successfully treated with argon plasma coagulation. His abdominal pain improved with tramadol, and his blood pressure was controlled by restarting lisinopril and continuing nadolol. He was monitored for alcohol withdrawal using the CIWA scale, which resolved without medication. The patient left the hospital against medical advice before a follow-up CBC was reviewed but was discharged on oral PPI, antihypertensives, and supportive medications with instructions to avoid alcohol and follow up with his primary and liver specialists.
